name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,818

entries.clue: Policeman having a threesome beginning to titillate fellow citizen (9)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is the letter it starts on, so only that opening letter of what follows is taken.

blocks.note: cop is the everyday word for a policeman
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
a trio is three of anything together
the first letter of that word, and nothing else of it

annotation.surface: A policeman who has joined a threesome and is beginning to enjoy himself.
annotation.walkthrough: The four pieces cut clean across the word's own seams: nothing in the clue points at the prefix co- or at the patriot behind it. 'Beginning to titillate' reads as part of the scene and is worth one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Co- means alongside, so the word names the patriot alongside you — somebody who shares your country, which is a fellow citizen.

entries.clue: Message bishop wearing lace pants (5)

indicatorNotes.wearing: Whatever you are wearing has you inside it, so the letter named before goes within the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.pants: 'Pants' is British slang for rubbish, and a word called rubbish is not left in the order it was written.

blocks.note: the four letters of the word in a new order
b is the bishop of a chess diagram

annotation.surface: A bishop caught wearing lace underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pants' does two jobs at once: the garment in the picture, and the British slang for rubbish that shuffles the letters beside it. The definition wants the telegram sense, the wire that carried news across the Atlantic.
annotation.definitionFit: A cable was the message sent abroad down a telegraph wire, and the word is still used for any dispatch sent that way.

entries.clue: Spooner's sexy apostle is in difficulty (7)

indicatorNotes.Spooner's: Spooner was the Oxford don remembered for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so anything of his asks you to make that swap.

blocks.note: sexy is 'fit' in British slang and the apostle is Paul, and trading the opening sounds of those two words spells something else

annotation.surface: A good-looking apostle who has landed himself in trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fit' for good-looking is British slang of the last few decades, and it is the half of the phrase the swap needs first. Say the pair aloud before trying to write anything down.
annotation.definitionFit: A pitfall was originally a covered pit dug to catch animals, so it is the difficulty you do not see until you are in it.

entries.clue: God, Norse, shows spine (5)

blocks.note: the hammer-wielding god of Norse myth
n is the label a dictionary puts on a word of Norse origin

annotation.surface: A Norse god showing some backbone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Norse' is asked to work twice over: it tells you which god is wanted, then hands over a letter of its own. The definition is botanical, not anatomical.
annotation.definitionFit: In botany a spine is the sharp woody point on a stem, which is what a thorn is on a rose or a blackthorn.

entries.clue: Begin perhaps boosting current king? Yes, in Madrid (7)

indicatorNotes.boosting: To boost a thing is to push it upwards, and in a down clue what goes up is read from the foot of the entry back to the top.

blocks.note: i is the symbol for electric current in a physics formula
Shakespeare's Lear, the king who split his kingdom between his daughters
si is yes in Spanish, and Madrid is named to point at the language

annotation.surface: Somebody in Madrid agreeing that the present king should be talked up.
annotation.walkthrough: Menachem Begin was prime minister of Israel, and 'perhaps' warns that the name is one instance of the answer rather than a synonym for it. 'Current' is the physicist's I, the letter on the other side of Ohm's law from the voltage.
annotation.definitionFit: Menachem Begin, who signed the Camp David accords as prime minister, was Israeli, so the name stands as one example of the nationality.

entries.clue: Setter confused over Unionist politician's memorial for the fallen? (4,5)

indicatorNotes.confused: Somebody confused has things out of order, and letters in that state come out in an order other than the one given.
indicatorNotes.over: In a down clue whatever is over something else is written above it, so the shuffled letters go in first and the rest below them.

blocks.note: the six letters of the clue's own word, rearranged
u is the Unionist in the name of a Northern Irish party on a ballot paper
an MP is the politician who sits in the House of Commons

annotation.surface: A setter baffled by a Unionist MP's war memorial.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter is not a person here but the word 'setter' itself, six letters waiting to be shuffled. The fallen of the definition are timber rather than soldiers, and the memorial is what the falling left behind.
annotation.definitionFit: What is left standing where a tree came down marks the spot for years afterwards, so it is a memorial to that fallen tree rather than to any war dead.

entries.clue: Perhaps something in miniscule fragment of pretty pottery (4)

indicatorNotes.fragment of: A fragment is a piece broken out of something bigger, so what is wanted is a short unbroken run inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: four letters in an unbroken run, starting inside the first word and stopping inside the second

annotation.surface: Something small spotted in a chip of pretty pottery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Miniscule' is spelt wrong on purpose — minuscule is the word — so the definition is pointing at the clue's own fourth word. The rest of the sentence is a hiding place, and 'fragment of' marks it.
annotation.definitionFit: A typo is a slip of the keyboard, and the clue's own 'miniscule' is one, so the definition names itself rather than describing anything else.

entries.clue: Combined, like some soup containing whiskey? (7)

indicatorNotes.containing: A tin containing soup has the soup inside it, so the letter named after this word goes within the letters before.

blocks.note: soup out of a tin is tinned soup
whiskey is W in the radio alphabet that starts Alpha, Bravo, Charlie

annotation.surface: Soup out of a tin with a slug of whiskey stirred into it.
annotation.walkthrough: Whiskey with an e is the radio alphabet's spelling, and that is the flag that one letter is wanted rather than a drink. The definition wants the participle two paired-off towns share.
annotation.definitionFit: Two things twinned are joined as a matching pair — as a British town is with one abroad — which is combined in the sense of yoked together.

entries.clue: Pregnancy hormone for good developing isn't blocked by drug (9)

indicatorNotes.developing: A developing situation is one still changing shape, so the letters it touches settle into a different order.
indicatorNotes.blocked by: A road blocked by a lorry has the lorry sitting in the middle of it, so the letter named goes in among the letters before.

blocks.note: somebody for a proposal is pro it
g is good on a school report
anagram fodder, four letters
e is ecstasy, the drug of a dance floor, and it joins the shuffle

annotation.surface: A hormone keeping a pregnancy safely on course even when a drug is taken.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For good' reads as permanently and is two separate pieces of wordplay. The answer is the manufactured form of progesterone, so the definition and the surface are talking about much the same thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A progestin is a synthetic progestogen, the hormone that keeps the womb lining ready for an embryo, so 'pregnancy hormone' names it by its job.

entries.clue: Austria hit by disorder returning in killers' domain (8)

indicatorNotes.returning: Something returning comes back the way it went, so those letters are read from the far end to the near one.

blocks.note: A is Austria on the oval sticker at the back of a car
to bat a ball is to hit it
a riot is public disorder, and its four letters run backwards here

annotation.surface: Austria hit by another outbreak of rioting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Killers' domain' is the slaughtermen's workplace rather than any den of murderers, and the apostrophe after the s says there is more than one of them. Austria's single letter is the one European cars carry.
annotation.definitionFit: An abattoir is a slaughterhouse, the building where animals are killed for meat, so the killers of the definition are the men working that floor.

entries.clue: Journalist's stream over, over, over at last (6)

indicatorNotes.over: A thing turned over lies the other way up, so the word beside it is read from its last letter back.
indicatorNotes.at last: What comes at last is the final one, so only the letter that word ends on is taken.

blocks.note: a tide is the stream of water running along a coast, and its letters run the other way here
o is the over on a cricket scoreboard
the letter that word ends on

annotation.surface: A journalist whose flow of words is finally finished.
annotation.walkthrough: Three overs in a row do three different jobs, the first of them turning the word before it round. The middle one is cricket's over, the six balls bowled from one end.
annotation.definitionFit: An editor is the journalist who runs the paper and cuts everyone else's copy, so the definition names the job by the trade it sits in.

entries.clue: Get back American trapped in African country undergoing revolution (6)

indicatorNotes.trapped in: Somebody trapped in a place cannot get out of it, so the letter named before goes inside the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.undergoing revolution: A revolution turns a thing full circle, so the letters assembled are read from the end back to the start.

blocks.note: Niger is the landlocked state on the southern edge of the Sahara
a is American on a form, the same single letter as in a film certificate

annotation.surface: An American held hostage in an African country in the middle of a coup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Undergoing revolution' is the country's politics in the surface and an instruction to read backwards in the wordplay. Niger and Nigeria are two separate countries, both named for the river that runs through them.
annotation.definitionFit: To regain a thing is to get it back after losing it — a title, your breath, your composure — so the two verbs match sense and tense.

entries.clue: Concentrates, being caught going in 3 directions, some more than once (8)

indicatorNotes.going in: What goes in ends up inside, so the letter named before it is written within the letters that follow.

blocks.note: east, south and north as their single letters, east and south each used more than once: E, S, S, E, N, E, S
c is caught on a cricket scorecard, the way a batsman's dismissal is written

annotation.surface: Somebody caught heading off in three directions, more than once.
annotation.walkthrough: The 3 is the number itself rather than a pointer to another clue, and the directions are compass points shrunk to single letters. 'Some more than once' is the licence to use two of them again.
annotation.definitionFit: An essence is the concentrated extract of a plant — vanilla essence, essence of rose — so the plural is concentrates in a cook's sense.

entries.clue: Confused tot supervised (6)

blocks.note: to tot up a column of figures is to add it
whoever supervised a party led it

annotation.surface: A muddled toddler being looked after.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tot' is the verb, totting up a bill, rather than the small child the rest of the sentence wants. Both pieces are past tense, which keeps them in step with the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An addled brain cannot think straight, the word having started out meaning rotten, as an addled egg is, so it is confused as an adjective.

entries.clue: Haggard book, perhaps, is something from the sewer? (5,4)

indicatorNotes.perhaps: 'Perhaps' flags an example, so the word before it stands for the wider class it belongs to rather than for itself.

blocks.note: a haggard face is a drawn one, tight and tired
a book is one of an author's works

annotation.surface: A Rider Haggard novel dredged up out of a drain.
annotation.walkthrough: The sewer is one who sews, not the drain, and the question mark is the only warning of it. Rider Haggard wrote King Solomon's Mines, which is why 'Haggard book' reads as a title rather than two separate words.
annotation.definitionFit: Drawn work is the openwork embroidery made by pulling threads out of a cloth, so it does come from a sewer in the needle-and-thread sense.

entries.clue: Maybe loon meets chap following a different path (9)

indicatorNotes.Maybe: 'Maybe' flags an example, so the bird named after it is one instance of the wider word wanted.

blocks.note: the waterbird North America calls a loon is the diver in Britain
a gent is a chap, the gentleman of a lavatory door cut short

annotation.surface: A lunatic running into a man who has taken another route.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loon' is the bird rather than the lunatic the surface offers, and the British name for it is the piece wanted. 'Following' looks like a positional instruction and is part of the definition instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Divergent paths are ones that separate and head off at their own angles, so anything divergent is following a different path.

entries.clue: Overwhelm single lady with vow of chastity at romantic encounter (8)

blocks.note: i is one in Roman numerals, and a single thing is one
a nun takes vows of poverty, chastity and obedience when she enters her order
an evening out with somebody you are courting is a date

annotation.surface: A single woman who has sworn off sex turning up for a date.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Single' is the numeral one, not the marital status the rest of the sentence pushes. The definition goes back to a Latin word for flooding, which is why it suits a river as readily as a person.
annotation.definitionFit: To inundate somebody is to flood them, with water or with letters and requests, which is to overwhelm them.

entries.clue: Chinese right-wing politician initially regrets the result of over-indulging (8)

indicatorNotes.initially: What is done initially is done first, so only the first letter of the word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: the Han are China's majority people, named after the dynasty
Michael Gove, the Conservative minister who ran the Cabinet Office and then edited The Spectator
the first letter of that word, and nothing else of it

annotation.surface: A right-wing Chinese politician regretting what he drank last night.
annotation.walkthrough: Gove is the Conservative crosswords reach for when four letters of right-wing politician are wanted. 'Initially' attaches to the word after it rather than to the politician, which is where the final letter comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: A hangover is the headache and nausea of the morning after too much drink, which is the result of over-indulging in its plainest form.

entries.clue: More magnificent kitchen implement picked up (7)

indicatorNotes.picked up: Something picked up is overheard rather than read, so what counts is the noise the word makes.

blocks.note: the tool you shred cheese on is a grater, and said aloud it is indistinguishable from the word wanted

annotation.surface: A finer kitchen gadget being lifted off the counter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' means overheard rather than lifted, and it is the only instruction in the clue. The two spellings sound alike because 'ea' and 'a' both come out as the long a of plate.
annotation.definitionFit: Greater is the comparative of great, so a greater hall or a greater name is the more magnificent one of two.

entries.clue: Got better recipe combined (7)

blocks.note: R is the recipe at the head of a prescription, Latin for 'take', still written on a doctor's pad
nations combined against an enemy are allied

annotation.surface: Somebody who has ended up with a better recipe by putting two together.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recipe' is the prescription abbreviation rather than the cookery sense the surface offers. The definition is a patient's recovery or a share price's, both of them in the past tense.
annotation.definitionFit: A patient rallies and so does a market, meaning each recovers, so the past tense of that verb is 'got better'.

entries.clue: Favourite pupil welcoming and unusually academic (6)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: To welcome somebody is to take them in, so the letters named after this word go inside the word before.
indicatorNotes.unusually: What is done unusually is not done the usual way, so those letters are not left in their usual order.

blocks.note: the teacher's pet is the favourite pupil
the three letters of the clue's own joining word, in another order

annotation.surface: A teacher's favourite who is welcoming and oddly scholarly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' joins nothing here: it is three letters to be rearranged, which is the hardest step in the clue to spot. A pet at school is a favourite rather than an animal.
annotation.definitionFit: A pedant parades small points of learning, so 'academic' names the type in its disparaging sense rather than as a job title.

entries.clue: Beasts of burden put on islands (7)

blocks.note: to don a coat is to put it on
the low coral islands strung out from the tip of Florida are the Keys

annotation.surface: Pack animals being put ashore on some islands.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put on' is the dressing verb, the one that goes with a hat, rather than anything to do with loading a cargo. The Keys take their name from cayo, the Spanish for a sandy islet.
annotation.definitionFit: A donkey carries panniers and packs where no cart can go, which is what makes it the beast of burden of the phrase.

entries.clue: Constituent of popular Tory leader with substantial backing (8)

indicatorNotes.leader: A party's leader stands at the head of it, so the letter wanted is the one its name starts on.
indicatorNotes.backing: Something backing away is travelling the other way, so those letters are written from the end towards the start.

blocks.note: a band that is popular this year is in
the first letter of the party's name
a substantial sum is a large one, and those five letters run backwards here

annotation.surface: A popular Tory leader with serious money behind him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' is the money in the surface and a turn-round instruction in the wordplay, which is the clue's one real disguise. Both definition and answer are adjectives about parts, not the calculus noun the word also serves as.
annotation.definitionFit: An integral part of a thing is one of the parts it is built from, which is what 'constituent' says of a component.

entries.clue: Rich, like lamb sauce? (6)

blocks.note: the British slang sense of being rolling in money
mint sauce is what British cooking puts beside roast lamb, so that sauce is flavoured this way

annotation.surface: A sauce for lamb with something rich about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma does all the hiding: it reads as a comparison and it is really the join between two separate definitions. The money sense comes from coins being minted.
annotation.definitionFit: Minted is British slang for rolling in money, and the sauce served with roast lamb is mint sauce, so it is minted in the kitchen sense.

entries.clue: Slogan of TV comedy originally ignored, then taken up (5)

indicatorNotes.originally ignored: What is ignored is left out, and a word's original letter is the one it starts on, so that opening letter never gets written.
indicatorNotes.taken up: In a down clue taking something up reads it from the foot of the entry towards the top, so those letters run backwards.

blocks.note: Bottom was the BBC sitcom of the early nineties with Rik Mayall and Adrian Edmondson sharing a squalid flat
the letter the sitcom's name starts on, dropped before anything else happens

annotation.surface: A comedy catchphrase nobody noticed at first that later caught on.
annotation.walkthrough: The comedy is Bottom, three series of two flatmates knocking each other about, and the clue turns entirely on knowing the title. 'Then' marks the order of the two operations, with the letter going before the turn.
annotation.definitionFit: A motto is the short phrase a school or a family lives by, which is a slogan in its formal, carved-over-the-door form.

entries.clue: Delighted if your hosts strengthen spiritually (5)

indicatorNotes.hosts: A host has guests staying inside the house, so the words before this one have the letters wanted sitting within them.

blocks.note: five letters in an unbroken run, starting inside the first word and stopping inside the last

annotation.surface: Delight at the people putting you up for the night.
annotation.walkthrough: The run starts late in the first word and stops early in the last, which is what keeps it out of sight. The definition is the church's sense of building somebody up, the Latin for 'build' sitting inside the word.
annotation.definitionFit: To edify is to build a person up morally — the word is the Latin for putting up a house — so it is strengthening of the inner kind.

entries.clue: He's too drunk to be calm (6)

indicatorNotes.drunk: A drunk man cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not stay in the line they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A man too far gone in drink to be talked down.
annotation.walkthrough: Two of the clue's five words are the fodder, which leaves 'drunk' to do the shuffling and nothing spare. 'Calm' is the verb here, what you do to somebody, not the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: To soothe a frightened child is to calm them, so the two verbs are plain synonyms taking the same sort of object.

entries.clue: Eccles printed out game (8)

indicatorNotes.out: Something out of true is not as it should be, so the letters it touches come out in an order other than their own.

blocks.note: Eccles is the name at the top of this puzzle, and the setter referring to himself is I
anagram fodder, the other seven letters

annotation.surface: Eccles printing a game out at his desk.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter who names himself in a clue is asking for the letter I, and Eccles is the pseudonym this puzzle is signed with. 'Game' is the adjective, as in game for anything.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody game for anything will take it on whatever the odds, which is what intrepid says of an explorer.

entries.clue: Broadcaster with radical culture (4)

blocks.note: Sky is the satellite broadcaster that carries much of British television
R stands for a radical in a chemist's formula, the group left unnamed

annotation.surface: A television company with a radical streak running through it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Culture' is the dairy sense, the bacteria that turn milk, rather than anything a broadcaster commissions. The answer is the thick soured milk Icelanders have eaten since Norse times, now sold in Britain as a high-protein yoghurt.
annotation.definitionFit: Skyr is the Icelandic soured-milk food set with a live starter, so 'culture' names it by the bacteria that make it what it is.

entries.clue: Solitude: year wasted in a boring manner (9)

indicatorNotes.wasted: A wasted evening has gone to pieces, and letters in pieces are put back in an order nobody chose.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
y is the year of a date or a mortgage term

annotation.surface: A year of solitude gone entirely to waste.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon is the join, with fodder on both sides of it and the definition left at the end. 'Wasted' reads as the fate of the year and is the word doing the shuffling.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done tediously drags on and bores whoever has to sit through it, which is doing it in a boring manner.
